eli5: Machines with sensors that send their readings to a computer automatically.
analogy: A fitness band, but for a machine.

eli5: One percentage for how close a machine gets to "perfect" production: always running, at full speed, with no bad parts. OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality [50].
analogy: A cricket batter's score: did they stay at the crease (availability), score fast (performance), and avoid getting out on bad shots (quality)?

eli5: Share of planned time the machine was actually running.
analogy: Share of a class period the teacher actually taught, not counting the projector breaking.

eli5: How fast it ran compared with its ideal speed.
analogy: Running a lap in 80 s when your best is 60 s gives 75%.

eli5: Share of parts that came out good.
analogy: Good rotis out of all rotis made.

eli5: OEE estimated from limited sensors, so not the full official version.
analogy: A thermometer reading taken by touching someone's forehead: useful, but not lab-grade.

eli5: The six ways a machine loses OEE: breakdowns, setup, minor stops, reduced speed, defects, and start-up losses [49].
analogy: Six leaks in a water tank.

eli5: Parts that have started but not yet finished.
analogy: Plates on the table at a canteen that have food but have not yet been eaten.

eli5: Finished parts per unit of time.
analogy: Students served per minute at the canteen counter.

eli5: How long one part takes from entering the line to leaving it. (Some people use "cycle time" for one station's time per part; say which one you mean.)
analogy: Your total wait from joining the queue to getting your food.

eli5: WIP = throughput × flow time. Know any two and you get the third [54][65].
analogy: 30 people in the queue, served at 2 per minute, so each waits about 15 minutes.

eli5: A rule that caps total WIP. A new part may enter only when a finished part leaves [52].
analogy: A club bouncer letting one person in only when one comes out.

eli5: Like CONWIP, but with a separate cap between each pair of stations [53].
analogy: A bouncer at every room in the club, not just the front door.

eli5: The slowest station, which limits the whole line.
analogy: The narrowest part of a bottle.

eli5: Find the bottleneck by checking which station works the longest without a break (not waiting for parts or space) [55].
analogy: Spotting the busiest cashier by who never gets a pause between customers.

eli5: Available time ÷ customer demand: the pace the line must keep. (unverified textbook definition, check before citing)
analogy: A metronome for the factory.

eli5: A bar chart sorted from biggest cause to smallest, usually showing a few causes do most of the damage.
analogy: Finding that 2 of your 10 subjects cause most of your stress.

eli5: A chart of a measurement over time, with upper and lower limits. Points outside the limits mean "something changed, check it" [60].
analogy: Your weekly weight chart with a "normal range" band.

eli5: Mean time between failures (how long it usually runs before breaking) and mean time to repair (how long fixing takes) [50].
analogy: How often your bike chain falls off, and how long it takes to put back.

eli5: A rugged small computer that controls a machine.
analogy: The Arduino's industrial big brother.

eli5: The operator's screen for watching and controlling machines, including alarms [1].
analogy: The dashboard and warning lights in a car.

eli5: A database built for time-stamped sensor readings [16][27].
analogy: A diary where every entry has the exact time written on it.

eli5: If the network drops, keep the data locally and send it later [1].
analogy: Writing a WhatsApp message offline; it sends when you get signal.

eli5: Doing the processing close to the machine instead of in a far-away cloud [4].
analogy: Cooking in your hostel room instead of ordering from across the city.

eli5: Software that runs the shop floor: releases orders, tells operators what to do, records what was made and traces each part [6].
analogy: The traffic police at a busy junction.

eli5: Manufacturing operations management: a wider version of MES that also covers quality, maintenance and inventory [1].
analogy: The whole traffic department, not just one officer.

eli5: Company-wide business software: orders, money, purchasing [11].
analogy: The college's admin office.

eli5: Advanced planning and scheduling: decides what to make, when, and on which machine, without overloading any machine [7].
analogy: A timetable maker who knows how many classrooms exist.

eli5: A standard that splits a factory's systems into levels, from sensors (level 0) up to business systems (level 4) [11].
analogy: A school's org chart: students, teachers, HOD, principal, management.

eli5: A standard that defines manufacturing KPIs and their formulas [51].
analogy: An official rulebook for how to calculate marks.

eli5: A central post office for data. Devices "publish" messages on topics, and apps "subscribe" to the topics they need [1].
analogy: A WhatsApp group: post once, everyone in it gets it.

eli5: A naming scheme for broker topics so every app agrees on where data lives, often following ISA-95 levels [1].
analogy: A postal address format everyone uses.

eli5: A computer model of a real system that stays updated with live data. If it runs only on assumed data, it is a simulation, not a twin [32][34].
analogy: A live cricket scorecard app versus a video game of cricket.

eli5: One connected data trail from design to production to use, so a change at one stage is visible at the others [10].
analogy: A shared Google Doc that everyone edits, versus emailing copies around.

eli5: A program that steps from event to event ("part arrives", "machine breaks") to predict how a line behaves [59].
analogy: Playing out a board game on paper to see who wins before playing for real.

eli5: A database of things and how they connect ("station 2 is part of line 1") [34].
analogy: A family tree.

eli5: A cheap microcontroller board like the Arduino, but with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in.
analogy: An Arduino that can send WhatsApp messages.

eli5: A chart that tracks a smoothed average, giving more weight to recent readings, so slow drifts show up early.
analogy: Judging a batter on recent form, not their whole career.

eli5: How many standard deviations a reading is away from normal. Big values mean unusual.
analogy: Scoring 95 when the class average is 60: clearly out of the ordinary.

eli5: A sensor that measures shaking and tilt.
analogy: The sensor that rotates your phone screen.

eli5: Time from starting the first job to finishing the last job in a batch.
analogy: How long the whole family's laundry takes, start to finish.

eli5: Simple job-ordering rules: first in, first out; or shortest job first.
analogy: A queue at the canteen vs letting the person buying only tea go first.

eli5: A timeline chart with one bar per job or machine, showing when each task runs.
analogy: A school timetable drawn as bars.

eli5: Running the same thing two ways under the same conditions and comparing results.
analogy: Trying two recipes on the same day for the same guests.

eli5: Precision: how many alarms were real. Recall: how many real problems got an alarm. F1 combines both.
analogy: A smoke alarm: does it beep for toast (precision), and does it ever miss a fire (recall)?

eli5: Two common machine-learning models for yes/no predictions. Logistic regression draws one boundary; a random forest votes across many decision trees.
analogy: One teacher's judgement vs a panel of judges voting.

eli5: A free Python library for discrete-event simulation.
analogy: A board game engine where you program the rules of your factory.

eli5: Google's free library for solving planning and scheduling problems.
analogy: A super-fast timetable maker.
